links.note: Tertullian of Carthage took up the New Prophecy's claims. He quotes a saying of the Paraclete given 'by the mouth of the prophetess Prisca'. In Against Praxeas he writes that his side withdrew from the 'carnally-minded' over the Paraclete.

links.note: Constantine sent an edict to the heretics, preserved in Eusebius's Life of Constantine. It names 'ye who are called Cataphrygians', a common name for the Montanists. It forbids their meetings and takes away the houses where they gathered.

links.note: Procopius, a hostile witness to Justinian, says the emperor ordered heresies such as the Montanists' to be given up. He reports that the Montanists of Phrygia shut themselves in their churches and burned them. A law of Justinian also names the Montanists.

sources.work: Procopius, Secret History XI (anonymous trans., Athenian Society 1896)
sources.quote: such as those of the Montanists and Sabbatians and all the others by which men's minds are led astray. Justinian ordered all these beliefs to be abandoned in favour of the old religion

links.note: Cyprian of Carthage refused communion to envoys who brought word that Novatian had been made bishop. He later wrote that Novatian 'is not in the Church'. Augustine asked whether repentance had been fully taught 'before the Novatians opposed'.

sources.work: Cyprian, Epistle 40 (ANF numbering), to Cornelius

sources.quote: Was repentance perfectly treated of before the Novatians opposed?

links.note: The eighth canon of the Council of Nicaea, in 325, set terms for receiving 'those who call themselves Cathari', the Novatianists. Their clergy had first to promise in writing to follow the teaching of the Catholic Church.

links.note: Constantine summoned Acesius, a Novatianist bishop, to the Council of Nicaea. Acesius told him the council had decided nothing new, yet kept his church apart. Socrates had the story from Auxanon, a Novatianist presbyter who went to Nicaea with Acesius.

sources.work: Socrates, Church History I.10 (trans. Zenos, NPNF 2.2)

links.note: Tertullian wrote five books Against Marcion. In them he attacks Marcion by name, charging that 'the heretic of Pontus introduces two Gods'.

links.note: Justin names Marcion of Pontus while Marcion was still alive, and charges him with teaching a god greater than the Creator. In his Dialogue with Trypho he lists the Marcians among groups who wrongly call themselves Christians.

sources.work: Justin, First Apology 26 (ANF 1)
sources.quote: And there is Marcion, a man of Pontus, who is even at this day alive, and teaching his disciples to believe in some other god greater than the Creator.

links.note: Eusebius of Caesarea finished his Church History around 324, under Constantine. In it he says the evil demon brought the Ebionites over to his own purposes. They were rightly named, he writes, for their 'poor and mean opinions concerning Christ'.

links.note: Jerome and Augustine wrote to each other across the sea for years. Augustine told Jerome of a bishop whose congregation rose up over the new wording of a line in Jonah. Jerome later wrote that he was resolved to love and respect Augustine and to defend his opinions as his own.

sources.quote: For my part, however, I am resolved to love you, to look up to you, to reverence and admire you, and to defend your opinions as my own.

links.note: Augustine urged Jerome to translate from the Greek Septuagint, not from the Hebrew. He feared the Latin and Greek churches would end up reading different Bibles. Even after Jerome died, he still held that no translator should be put above the Seventy.
